individuel.explanation: "Individuel" means "individual". It comes from the noun "et individ" (an individual person). To describe a talk that is meant for just one person, put it before the noun: "en individuel samtale" (an individual conversation).

indlysende.explanation: "Indlysende" means "obvious". To say that a fact is clear to everyone, use it after "Det er": "Det er indlysende, at han tager fejl" (It is obvious that he is wrong).

indre.explanation: "Indre" means "inner". To talk about the central part of a city, say "den indre by" (the inner city). To talk about feelings inside a person, say "indre uro" (inner unrest).

indsigt.explanation: "En indsigt" means "an insight". To say what a person understands well, put "i" (in) after it: "Hun har god indsigt i økonomi" (She has good insight into economics).

indtil.explanation: "Indtil" means "until". To say when something stops, put a time after it: "indtil fredag" (until Friday). To say something lasts until an event happens, put a whole sentence after it: "Bliv, indtil du er rask" (Stay until you are well).

indtil nu.explanation: "Indtil nu" means "until now". It is built from "indtil" (until) and "nu" (now). To talk about what happens from this moment forward, use "fra nu af" (from now on): "Fra nu af kommer jeg i tide" (From now on I will be on time).

indtil videre.explanation: "Indtil videre" means "so far". It is built from "indtil" (until) and "videre" (further). To talk about the coming days, it means "for now": "Vi holder lukket indtil videre" (We are staying closed for now).

indviklet.explanation: "Indviklet" means "complicated". It comes from the verb "at indvikle" (to wrap up), so something "indviklet" is wrapped up in itself and hard to follow.

ineffektiv.explanation: "Ineffektiv" means "inefficient". It is built from "effektiv" (efficient) with "in" in front, which turns it into the opposite. To say that a medicine does not give the result you want, use it for the medicine: "en ineffektiv medicin" (an ineffective medicine).

inficeret.explanation: "Inficeret" means "infected". It comes from the verb "at inficere" (to infect). To say that a person has caught an illness, use "smittet" (infected) instead: "Han er smittet" (He is infected).

inflation.explanation: "Inflation" means "inflation". To say that prices are going up, use the verb "at stige" (to rise): "Inflationen stiger" (Inflation is rising).

influenza.explanation: "Influenza" means "flu". To say you have the flu, leave out "en" (a): "Jeg har influenza" (I have the flu).

information.explanation: "Information" means "information". To say what the information is about, put "om" (about) after it: "information om togene" (information about the trains).

informeret.explanation: "Informeret" means "informed". It comes from the verb "at informere" (to inform). To name the topic you know about, use "om" (about): "Er du informeret om ændringen?" (Are you informed about the change?)

ingefær.explanation: "Ingefær" means "ginger". To name a drink made with ginger, put "ingefær" in front of the drink: "ingefærte" (ginger tea) and "ingefærøl" (ginger beer).

ingen.explanation: "Ingen" means "no one". To say you have none of something, use it before the noun, as "no": "Der er ingen billetter" (There are no tickets). Danish does not add "ikke" (not) next to it, so say "Jeg kender ingen her" (I know no one here). In a question, use "nogen" (anyone) instead: "Er der nogen hjemme?" (Is anyone home?)

ingen problemer.explanation: "Ingen problemer" means "no problem". To agree when someone asks you for a small favor, say it as your answer: "Kan jeg få en pose?" "Ingen problemer." (Can I have a bag? No problem.) A longer way to say the same is "Det er ikke noget problem" (That is not a problem).

ingen årsag.explanation: "Ingen årsag" means "don't mention it". Literally, it says "no reason". To answer when someone thanks you, say it as your reply: "Tak for lånet." "Ingen årsag." (Thanks for the loan. Don't mention it.)

ingenting.explanation: "Ingenting" means "nothing". To say you see something, use "noget" (something): "Jeg ser noget" (I see something). Danish does not add "ikke" (not) next to "ingenting", so say "Jeg ved ingenting" (I know nothing). To say that no person is there, use "ingen" (no one): "Ingen er her" (No one is here).

inklusive.explanation: "Inklusive" means "including". To list what a price covers, put it before the item: "inklusive fragt" (including shipping). It can also come after the item: "Morgenmad inklusive" (Breakfast included).

inspireret.explanation: "Inspireret" means "inspired". To name the person or thing that inspired you, add "af" (by) after it: "inspireret af en bog" (inspired by a book).

intakt.explanation: "Intakt" means "intact". English speakers should spell it with "kt" at the end, not "ct". To say a delivered package is not damaged, say: "Pakken er intakt" (The package is intact).

intelligens.explanation: "En intelligens" means "an intelligence". It is the noun for the describing word "intelligent" (intelligent).

intelligent.explanation: "Intelligent" means "intelligent". It is the describing word for the noun "intelligens" (intelligence). To say an animal shows good thinking, use it before the noun: "en intelligent hund" (an intelligent dog).

interessant.explanation: "Interessant" means "interesting". To say something sounds interesting, use "lyder" (sounds): "Det lyder interessant" (That sounds interesting). To say you are interested, use "interesseret" (interested) instead: "Jeg er interesseret i musik" (I am interested in music).

interesseret.explanation: "Interesseret" means "interested". To say what you are interested in, put "i" (in) after it: "Hun er interesseret i historie" (She is interested in history).

interesseret i.explanation: "Interesseret i" means "interested in". To say you are interested in doing something, put "at" (to) and a verb after it: "interesseret i at lære" (interested in learning).

intern.explanation: "Intern" means "internal". To talk about messages that stay inside a company, say "intern kommunikation" (internal communication).

international.explanation: "International" means "international". To talk about something inside one country, use "national" (national) instead: "en national turnering" (a national tournament).

internet.explanation: "Internet" means "the internet". To say that a place has no connection, use it for the connection: "Der er ikke internet her" (There is no internet here).

intet.explanation: "Intet" means "no". Use it before a word that takes "et": "Det er intet problem" (It is no problem). To say you see nothing, it also means "nothing" after the verb: "Jeg ser intet" (I see nothing).

intetkøn.explanation: "Et intetkøn" means "a neuter gender". It is built from "intet" (nothing) and "et køn" (a gender), so it literally means "no gender". Words in this group take "et", as in "et hus" (a house) and "et barn" (a child).

involveret.explanation: "Involveret" means "involved". To name what a person takes part in, put "i" (in) after it: "Hun er involveret i projektet" (She is involved in the project).

ironisk.explanation: "Ironisk" means "ironic". It is the describing word for the noun "en ironi" (an irony). To say a situation turned out the opposite of what you would expect, say: "Det er ironisk, at bageren aldrig spiser brød" (It is ironic that the baker never eats bread).

irrationel.explanation: "Irrationel" means "irrational". English speakers should end it in "el", not "al". In math, to name a number that cannot be written as a simple fraction, say "et irrationelt tal" (an irrational number).

irrelevant.explanation: "Irrelevant" means "irrelevant". To name the matter that something does not concern, put "for" (for) after it: "Det er irrelevant for sagen" (It is irrelevant to the case).

irriterende.explanation: "Irriterende" means "annoying". To say that you are the one who feels bothered, use "irriteret" (irritated) instead: "Jeg er irriteret" (I am irritated).

irriteret.explanation: "Irriteret" means "irritated". To say what causes the feeling, use "irriterende" (annoying) instead: "Lyden er irriterende" (The sound is annoying).

is.explanation: "Is" means "ice cream". To order one scoop, say "en kugle is" (a scoop of ice cream, literally "a ball of ice cream"). To say there is frozen water on the road, use it for "ice": "Der er is på vejen" (There is ice on the road).

ishockey.explanation: "Ishockey" means "ice hockey". It is built from "is" (ice) and "hockey" (hockey). To say you watch a game on TV, use "at se" (to watch): "Vi ser ishockey i aften" (We are watching ice hockey tonight).

iskold.explanation: "Iskold" means "ice-cold". It is built from "is" (ice) and "kold" (cold).

islam.explanation: "Islam" means "Islam". English writes "Islam" with a big first letter, but Danish writes "islam" like an ordinary word. To name a person who follows it, use "en muslim" (a Muslim).

island.explanation: "Island" means "Iceland". Do not mix it up with the English word "island". To say an island, use "en ø" (an island): "en lille ø" (a small island).

islandsk.explanation: "Islandsk" means "Icelandic". It comes from "Island" (Iceland). To name the language, use it as the language: "Hun taler islandsk" (She speaks Icelandic).

isolation.explanation: "Isolation" means "isolation". To talk about keeping heat inside a house, use "isolering" (insulation) instead: "isolering af loftet" (insulation of the attic).

isoleret.explanation: "Isoleret" means "isolated". To say a house keeps its heat, use it to mean "insulated": "et godt isoleret hus" (a well-insulated house).

isolering.explanation: "Isolering" means "insulation". To talk about people kept apart from others, use "isolation" (isolation) instead: "Patienten er i isolation" (The patient is in isolation).

isslag.explanation: "Isslag" means "freezing rain". It is built from "is" (ice) and "slag" (a blow, a hit).

især.explanation: "Især" means "especially". To pick out one case from a group you just named, put "især" after the group: "Jeg holder af dyr, især hunde" (I like animals, especially dogs).

italien.explanation: "Italien" means "Italy". To describe things from Italy, use "italiensk" (Italian) instead: "italiensk mad" (Italian food).

italiensk.explanation: "Italiensk" means "Italian". It comes from "Italien" (Italy). To name the language, use it as the language: "Jeg taler italiensk" (I speak Italian).

ivrig.explanation: "Ivrig" means "eager". To say someone does a hobby with great energy, put it before the noun: "en ivrig cyklist" (a keen cyclist).

iøjnefaldende.explanation: "Iøjnefaldende" means "conspicuous". It comes from "at falde i øjnene" (literally, to fall into the eyes).

at jage.explanation: "At jage" means "to hunt / chase". To say someone runs after a person to catch them, use it for the chase: "Politiet jager tyven" (The police chase the thief). To say someone hunts wild animals, use it for the hunt: "Han jager hjorte" (He hunts deer).

at jamre.explanation: "At jamre" means "to wail / whine". To say what someone complains about, put "over" (about) after it: "Han jamrer over vejret" (He whines about the weather).

at juble.explanation: "At juble" means "to cheer". It is the verb for the noun "en jubel" (jubilation). To say when people cheer, add a sentence with "når" (when): "Folk jubler, når holdet scorer" (People cheer when the team scores).

at justere.explanation: "At justere" means "to adjust". Do not copy the "ad" of "adjust": the Danish word starts with "ju". To say you change a plan a little, put the plan after it: "Vi justerer planen" (We are adjusting the plan).

en jagt.explanation: "En jagt" means "a hunt". It is the noun for the verb "at jage" (to chase). To talk about looking hard for something, use "jagten på" (the hunt for): "jagten på en bolig" (the hunt for a home).

en jakke.explanation: "En jakke" means "a jacket". To talk about a long, warm coat instead, use "en frakke" (a coat): "Jeg tager frakken på" (I put my coat on).

en japaner.explanation: "En japaner" means "a Japanese person". To describe things from Japan, use "japansk" (Japanese) instead: "japansk te" (Japanese tea).

en jobannonce.explanation: "En jobannonce" means "a job ad". It is built from "job" (job) and "en annonce" (an ad).

en jobsamtale.explanation: "En jobsamtale" means "a job interview". It is built from "job" (job) and "en samtale" (a conversation). To say you are going to one, use "til" (to): "Jeg skal til jobsamtale" (I am going to a job interview).

en joke.explanation: "En joke" means "a joke". To say you tell one, use "at fortælle" (to tell): "Han fortæller en joke" (He tells a joke). To say you are not serious, use "at lave sjov" (to kid around): "Jeg laver bare sjov" (I am just joking).

en jomfru.explanation: "En jomfru" means "a virgin / maiden". To name the mother of Jesus, use it in "Jomfru Maria" (the Virgin Mary). To name the star sign, use "Jomfruen" (Virgo).

en jordemoder.explanation: "En jordemoder" means "a midwife". It is built from "jord" (earth) and "moder" (mother). In Denmark, a "jordemoder" leads a normal birth, and a doctor joins only if there are problems.

en jordnød.explanation: "En jordnød" means "a peanut". It is built from "jord" (ground) and "en nød" (a nut).

en journal.explanation: "En journal" means "a medical record". To say a diary instead, use "en dagbog" (a diary): "Jeg skriver i min dagbog" (I write in my diary).

en journalist.explanation: "En journalist" means "a journalist". To name the job, put "som" (as) before it: "Hun arbejder som journalist" (She works as a journalist).

en juleferie.explanation: "En juleferie" means "a Christmas vacation". It is built from "jul" (Christmas) and "ferie" (vacation). To say you are on vacation, use "ferie" as its own word: "Jeg har ferie" (I am on vacation).

en julefrokost.explanation: "En julefrokost" means "a Christmas lunch". It is built from "jul" (Christmas) and "frokost" (lunch). In Denmark, a "julefrokost" is a big get-together in December with food and drinks.

en julegave.explanation: "En julegave" means "a Christmas present". It is built from "jul" (Christmas) and "en gave" (a gift). To thank someone for any gift, use "gave" as its own word: "Tak for gaven!" (Thanks for the gift!)

en julemand.explanation: "En julemand" means "a Santa Claus". It is built from "jul" (Christmas) and "mand" (man). To make other Christmas words, put "jul" in front: "et julekort" (a Christmas card).

en julemiddag.explanation: "En julemiddag" means "a Christmas dinner". It is built from "jul" (Christmas) and "middag" (dinner). To talk about a Christmas lunch party instead, use "en julefrokost" (a Christmas lunch): "Vi har julefrokost på arbejdet" (We have a Christmas lunch at work).

en julesang.explanation: "En julesang" means "a Christmas carol". It is built from "jul" (Christmas) and "sang" (song). The part "sang" also appears in "en børnesang" (a children's song).

en julestjerne.explanation: "En julestjerne" means "a poinsettia". It is built from "jul" (Christmas) and "en stjerne" (a star). To talk about a star decoration, it also means "a Christmas star": "Vi hænger en julestjerne op i vinduet" (We hang a Christmas star in the window).

en jungle.explanation: "En jungle" means "a jungle". To talk about a confusing mess of things, use it as a picture: "en jungle af regler" (a jungle of rules).

en jurist.explanation: "En jurist" means "a legal professional". It comes from "jura" (law as a subject). To name the person who argues a case in court, use "en advokat" (a lawyer): "Jeg ringer til en advokat" (I am calling a lawyer).

en jury.explanation: "En jury" means "a jury". To say a person is a member, use "sidde i" (to sit in): "Hun sidder i juryen" (She is on the jury).

en jyde.explanation: "En jyde" means "a Jutlander". It comes from "Jylland" (Jutland), the part of Denmark that is connected to Germany. The dialect of Jutland is called "jysk" (Jutlandic).

en jæger.explanation: "En jæger" means "a hunter". In Denmark, a hunter must have "et jagttegn" (a hunting license).

en jætte.explanation: "En jætte" means "a giant". In Denmark, ancient stone burial chambers are called "jættestuer" (giants' chambers), because people once believed giants built them.

en jøde.explanation: "En jøde" means "a Jew". To say Jewish, use "jødisk" (Jewish) instead: "jødisk mad" (Jewish food).

et jakkesæt.explanation: "Et jakkesæt" means "a suit". It is built from "jakke" (jacket) and "sæt" (set). To talk about things that belong together, use "et sæt" (a set): "et sæt bestik" (a set of silverware).

et job.explanation: "Et job" means "a job". To say you got a new position, say: "Jeg har et nyt job" (I have a new job). To say you are going to the place where you work, use "arbejde" (work) instead: "Jeg skal på arbejde" (I am going to work).

et jobcenter.explanation: "Et jobcenter" means "a job center". In Denmark, a "jobcenter" is run by the local council and helps people without work find a job and get financial support.

et jordbær.explanation: "Et jordbær" means "a strawberry". It is built from "jord" (earth, ground) and "et bær" (a berry). To talk about soil, use "jord" as its own word: "Planten står i jord" (The plant is in the soil).

et jordskælv.explanation: "Et jordskælv" means "an earthquake". It is built from "jord" (earth) and "skælv" (a tremble). To say a person trembles, use the verb "at skælve" (to tremble): "Han skælver af kulde" (He trembles from cold).

et jubilæum.explanation: "Et jubilæum" means "an anniversary". To name a round number of years for a club, use it with the number: "Klubben har 50-års jubilæum" (The club has its 50-year anniversary). To name a couple's wedding anniversary, use "en bryllupsdag" (a wedding anniversary) instead: "I dag er det vores bryllupsdag" (Today is our wedding anniversary).

et julesalg.explanation: "Et julesalg" means "a Christmas sale". It is built from "jul" (Christmas) and "salg" (sale).

et juletræ.explanation: "Et juletræ" means "a Christmas tree". It is built from "jul" (Christmas) and "et træ" (a tree). To make other Christmas words, put "jul" in front: "et julekort" (a Christmas card).

ja.explanation: "Ja" means "yes". To accept an offer politely, add "tak" (thanks): "Ja, tak" (Yes, please). To answer yes to a question that has "ikke" (not) in it, say "jo" (yes) instead: "Kommer du ikke?" "Jo." (Aren't you coming? Yes, I am.)

jalousi.explanation: "Jalousi" means "jealousy". English speakers should note the spelling: it has no "e" and ends in "i". The describing word is "jaloux" (jealous): "Han er jaloux" (He is jealous).

jaloux.explanation: "Jaloux" means "jealous". To name the person you are jealous of, put "på" (of) after it: "Hun er jaloux på sin kollega" (She is jealous of her coworker).

jaloux på.explanation: "Jaloux på" means "jealous of". To say you want what someone has, say: "Jeg er jaloux på din nye bil" (I am jealous of your new car). To say you fear someone will take a person you love, say: "Han er jaloux på hendes ven" (He is jealous of her friend).

jamen.explanation: "Jamen" means "but". To object to what someone said, start your reply with it: "Jamen, det passer ikke!" (But that is not true!) To ask why something is not so, it means "well": "Jamen, hvorfor ikke?" (Well, why not?)

januar.explanation: "Januar" means "January". To say in which month something happens, use "i" (in): "Jeg har fødselsdag i januar" (My birthday is in January). English speakers should spell it with no "y" at the end.

japan.explanation: "Japan" means "Japan". To describe things from Japan, use "japansk" (Japanese) instead: "japansk te" (Japanese tea).

japansk.explanation: "Japansk" means "Japanese". It comes from "Japan" (Japan). To name the language, use it as the language: "Jeg taler japansk" (I speak Japanese).

jaså.explanation: "Jaså" means "is that so". To answer news that surprises you, say it as your reply: "Jeg har købt en hund." "Jaså!" (I have bought a dog. Is that so!)

javel.explanation: "Javel" means "I see". To show you have heard what someone said, say it as your reply: "Jeg er flyttet." "Javel." (I have moved. I see.)
